tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__find
tools.description: Search the current page in the Browser pane for elements whose accessibility-tree line (role / name / text) contains `query`, case-insensitively. Returns up to 20 `ref_N` matches usable with `computer`/`form_input`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

query.description: Text to look for in an element's role, name or text (case-insensitive substring, e.g. "Sign in", "search", "Add to cart").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__form_input
tools.description: Set the value of a form element identified by `ref` (from read_page/find). Handles input/textarea/select/checkbox/contenteditable.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

ref.description: Element reference ID from the read_page tool (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2")

value.description: The value to set. For checkboxes use boolean, for selects use option value or text, for other inputs use appropriate string/number

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this form fill does on the page and to what, for example 'Sets the delivery date to 29 September'. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__get_page_text
tools.description: Extract the visible text of the Browser pane's page (article/main content first, falls back to body innerText).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__javascript_tool
tools.description: Execute JavaScript in the Browser pane's page for DEBUGGING and INSPECTION only. Do NOT use this to implement UI changes — edit source code instead.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description: Action to perform (only `javascript_exec` is supported).

text.description: The JavaScript code to execute. Evaluated in the page context with REPL semantics: top-level `await` works, and the result of the last expression is returned automatically — write the expression you want (e.g. `window.myData.value`, or `await fetch(url).then(r=>r.json())`) rather than `return ...`. Return values are serialized as JSON.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__navigate
tools.description: Navigate the Browser pane to a URL, or go "back"/"forward" in history. If the Browser pane isn't open yet, this opens it at the URL (no dev server needed).

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

url.description: The URL to navigate to. Can be provided with or without protocol (defaults to https://). Use "forward" to go forward in history or "back" to go back in history.

force.description: If the page shows a "Leave site?" dialog because of unsaved changes, discard those changes and navigate anyway. Defaults to false.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_list
tools.description: List servers started with preview_start. Returns serverIds for use with other preview_* tools.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_logs
tools.description: Get server stdout/stderr output. Use to check for build errors, verify server behavior, or read debug output. Use 'level' to filter to errors only, or 'search' to filter for specific text. Use after preview_start.

level.description: Filter by level: 'all' (default) shows all output, 'error' shows only lines containing error/exception/failed/fatal

search.description: Filter to lines containing this text (e.g., '[DEBUG]', 'POST /api')

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_start

name.description: Server name from .claude/launch.json.

url.description: URL to open in the Browser pane without a dev server (instead of starting one by `name`).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__preview_stop
tools.description: Stop a server started with preview_start.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_console_messages
tools.description: Get console output (log, info, warn, error, debug) from the Browser pane.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

limit.description: Max entries to return (default: 50, max: 200).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_network_requests
tools.description: List network requests, or fetch a specific response body by `requestId`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

urlPattern.description: Substring filter on the request URL as listed (auth values show as REDACTED).

requestId.description: If provided, returns the response body for this request instead of listing.

limit.description: Max entries to return when listing (default: 50).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__read_page
tools.description: Read the current page in the Browser pane as a YAML-style accessibility tree. Each interactive element is tagged `[ref_N]` for use with `computer`/`form_input`/`find`. Prefer this over screenshot for verifying text and structure. Output is limited to 50000 characters by default; if it exceeds the limit it is truncated with a note — pass a larger max_chars, or use ref_id/depth to focus.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

filter.description: 'interactive' returns only clickable/typable elements; 'all' (default) returns the full tree.

ref_id.description: Restrict the tree to descendants of this `ref_N` (from a previous read_page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_close
tools.description: Close one Browser pane tab. Closing the last tab closes the Browser pane itself (reopen it with `preview_start`).

tabId.description: Tab to close.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_context
tools.description: List every Browser pane tab (origin only — titles are page-authored). Returns {browserOpen, tabs: [{tabId, origin, isActive}]} plus a line saying whether the pane is currently displayed or hidden (a hidden pane still works, but its page runs as a background page, so timing and performance numbers from it can be off; prefer `read_page` / `get_page_text` over screenshots while it is hidden). browserOpen is false (and tabs empty) until `preview_start` or `navigate` opens the pane, so you don't need to call this before opening it.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_create
tools.description: Open a fresh blank Browser pane tab; returns the new tabId. Opens in the background by default — set `foreground: true` when the user wants to watch. Prefer `preview_start` with a `url` when you know the destination; use `navigate` to load a URL into a blank tab.

foreground.description: Front the new tab (user asked to see it or is following along). Default false: open behind the user's current tab.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__tabs_select
tools.description: Front the given Browser pane tab. Background tabs keep running while you drive them, so front one only when the user should look — or for a page that pauses itself while hidden (e.g. a video player).

tabId.description: Tab to front.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_iOS_Simulator__control
tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

tools.name: mcp__visualize__show_widget
tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

questions.question:
Round 1 | Part: Solo bill | Targeting: Goal | Why now: "manage their own bill alone" could mean a one-time calculation or keeping a record over time, and that choice shapes the whole app | Ambiguity: ~68%

When one person uses the app alone, what are they doing?

Cause → effect:
• One-time check (like a calculator): enter a bill, see the total with tax/tip, done. Effect: no storage needed, so the app can run entirely in the browser with no server or database. Simplest to set up from the README and fewest things that can break.
• Keep a history of past bills: bills are saved and can be revisited. Effect: the app needs storage (in the browser or a local server + database), which means more setup steps, more acceptance criteria (saving, editing, deleting) and more ways things can go wrong.
• Both: one-time by default, with saving as an extra. Effect: bigger first version. Saving can be marked Not implemented at first.

options.description: Enter the bill, see the result, nothing saved. Keeps the app simple, fully in-browser, and easy for reviewers to run.

options.label: Keep a history
options.description: Save bills to look back at later. Adds storage, setup steps and more stories to test.

options.label: One-time now, history later
options.description: Build one-time first. Write the saving stories now but mark them Not implemented.

content.thinking: Round 1 wrapped up with a 64% ambiguity score — we still need to pin down how tax/tip/shared dishes are split and where bill history gets stored. Next up, I'll dig into the itemized split logic itself, since those rules determine what each person owes.

questions.question:
Round 2 | Part: Itemized split | Targeting: Goal | Why now: when everyone pays for what they ordered, the rule for tax and tip changes each person's total | Ambiguity: 64%

Example: Ali orders a $40 steak, Sara orders a $10 salad. Tax is $5 and tip is $10. How should the $15 of tax and tip be shared?

Cause → effect:
• In proportion to what each ordered: Ali pays 80% of tax/tip ($12), Sara pays 20% ($3). Totals are $52 and $13. Fairest, and it matches how a restaurant charges tax.
• Split equally: each pays $7.50. Totals are $47.50 and $17.50. Simple to explain, but the person who ordered less subsidizes the big spender.
• Let the group choose each time: a switch on the bill. Most flexible, but it doubles the cases to test and explain.

options.label: Proportional (Recommended)
options.description: Each person's share of tax and tip matches their share of the food. Fairest, and what most bill-splitting apps do.

options.label: Split equally
options.description: Everyone pays the same tax and tip regardless of what they ordered. Simpler, but less fair.

options.label: Group chooses each time
options.description: A setting on each bill. Most flexible, but more to build and test.

content.thinking: Round 2 scoring puts ambiguity at 58.5%, with gaps remaining in shared-dish/rounding handling, constraint details, and testable success criteria. Next I'll dig into tech choices and storage setup, since the history feature determines where data lives and how reviewers will run the app.

questions.question:
Round 3 | Part: Tech choices and local setup | Targeting: Constraints | Why now: saved history needs a home, and that home decides whether reviewers need to start a server | Ambiguity: 58.5%

No cloud services are allowed, so history can only live on the user's own computer. Where should saved bills live?

Cause → effect:
• Inside the browser: bills are saved by Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Safari itself. Effect: no server at all. The README is just "install, start, open the page". But bills stay in that one browser: clearing browsing data or switching browsers loses them, and Safari can wipe data from sites you haven't visited in a while.
• In a small local server with a database file: the app runs a backend on your computer that saves bills to a file in the project folder. Effect: history survives browser clearing and is shared by every browser on that computer. But the README needs an extra install step and a start command, and there's more code (a backend plus its API) to build and test.
• Browser storage plus export/import: browser storage, plus a button to download your bills as a file and load them back. Effect: still no server, and users can back up their own data.

options.label: Local server + database (Recommended)
options.description: Bills saved to a file on your computer by a small backend. History survives browser clearing; the README gets one extra step. Also gives you a real frontend and backend to choose technologies for.

options.label: Browser storage only
options.description: Simplest to run, no backend. History can be lost if browser data is cleared.

options.label: Browser storage + export/import
options.description: No backend, and users can back up and restore their bills as a file.

questions.question:
Round 4 | Part: Equal split + Solo bill | Targeting: Goal | Challenge mode | Why now: we've treated solo, equal and itemized as three separate modes, but that may be an assumption rather than a need | Ambiguity: 51.3%

What if the app has just ONE kind of bill instead of three modes?
• A solo bill is a bill with 1 person.
• An equal split is a bill where every item is shared by everyone.
• An itemized split is a bill where each item is assigned to the person (or people) who had it.

Cause → effect:
• One bill, people optional: one screen to learn and one calculation that can be tested very thoroughly. A shared appetizer works naturally, and history stores one kind of record. A bill can even mix 'my own items' and 'shared items'. The downside: a quick 'split $90 three ways' takes a few more taps unless we add a shortcut.
• Three separate modes: each mode is simpler on its own and the quick equal split is instant. But there are three sets of screens, rules and stories to build and test, and you can't easily mix them (e.g. itemized plus a shared appetizer).

questions.question:
Round 5 | Part: Equal split | Targeting: Success criteria | Why now: you said the app must never give a wrong result, and rounding is where splits usually go wrong | Ambiguity: 47.9%

Example: a $100.00 bill split 3 ways is $33.333… each, which can't be paid in cents. What should the app show?

Cause → effect:
• Shares add up exactly: two people pay $33.33 and one pays $33.34, and the app says who pays the extra cent. Effect: the shares always add up to exactly $100.00. That's easy to test ("the shares always add up to the bill"), and nobody under- or over-pays.
• Everyone rounds up: each pays $33.34 and the group collects $100.02. Effect: the bill is always covered and everyone pays the same, but the group overpays by a few cents, which is technically a wrong total.
• Everyone rounds down + warning: each pays $33.33 and the app shows "1 cent short". Effect: equal amounts, but someone has to cover the gap by hand.

options.label: Shares add up exactly (Recommended)
options.description: Leftover cents go to some people, and the app shows who. The total always matches the bill to the cent.

options.label: Everyone rounds up
options.description: Equal shares that slightly overpay. The bill is always covered, but the total doesn't match exactly.

options.label: Round down + show shortfall
options.description: Equal shares, and the app says how many cents are still missing.

Round 6 | Part: Itemized split | Targeting: Goal | Simplify mode | Why now: shared dishes are the biggest open question in itemized mode, and the simplest answer may be enough | Ambiguity: 43.6%

In itemized mode, can one item belong to more than one person? Example: a $12 nachos plate shared by Ali, Sara and Omar.

Cause → effect:
• Yes, items can be shared: when adding an item you tick who had it, and its cost is split evenly between them ($4 each). Effect: handles real dinners with shared plates. Needs the same leftover-cent rule as equal split, and there's a bit more on the screen to build and test.
• No, one owner per item: each item belongs to exactly one person. Effect: simpler screen and calculation, but shared dishes have to be handled by hand (e.g. typing in 3 items at $4), which is awkward when the price doesn't divide evenly.
• One owner per item, plus a 'shared by everyone' option: an item is either one person's or split by the whole table. Effect: covers the common 'starters for the table' case without picking people per item.

How should someone enter tax and tip?

Cause → effect:
• Either a % or an amount, for each: a small switch next to tax and next to tip. Effect: works whether your receipt shows "Tax $4.13" or you think "tip 15%". There are more cases to test (4 combinations), and the app must reject things like a 150% tip or a negative tax.
• Percent only: type 8% tax, 15% tip. Effect: simple, but if the receipt shows tax as a dollar amount, the user has to work out the % themselves, which can lead to small rounding errors.
• Amount only: type $4.13 tax, $10 tip. Effect: matches the receipt exactly, but tipping by % means doing the math yourself.
• Also: should a tip be optional (0 allowed)? I'll assume yes.

Should the app enforce these limits? Anything outside them gets a clear message next to the field, and no result is shown until it's fixed:
• Money: from $0.01 to $1,000,000, at most 2 decimal places. No negatives, letters or blanks.
• People: whole numbers from 2 to 50 for group splits. 0 people (division by zero), 1, 2.5, and -3 are all rejected.
• Tax and tip %: 0% to 100%.
• One currency: amounts are plain numbers shown with 2 decimals, with no currency conversion.

Cause → effect:
• With these limits: every edge case has a defined answer, so each one becomes a clear acceptance criterion (e.g. "Given 0 people, when I calculate, then I see 'Enter at least 2 people'"). Huge or tiny numbers can never produce strange results.
• No upper limits: more freedom, but extremely large numbers can lose accuracy or overflow the screen, and the 'never a wrong result' promise gets harder to test.
• Different numbers: tell me your own limits (e.g. up to 100 people, or a $10,000 maximum).

Which building blocks should the app use? Here's what each choice means in practice:

• JavaScript/TypeScript everywhere: React for the screens, Node.js (Express) for the small server, SQLite (a single database file) for history, and automated tests that click through the app in real Chrome/Firefox/Safari engines. Effect: reviewers install one free thing (Node.js), and the README is about 3 commands. One language for the whole project, and the most common web setup, with lots of help online.

• Python server + React screens: Python (FastAPI) for the server, React for the screens, SQLite for history. Effect: reviewers install two things (Python and Node.js), so the README is longer and there are two languages to learn. Good if you already know or want to learn Python.

• Python only, simple pages: Python (Flask) builds the pages itself, with a little plain JavaScript. Effect: one install (Python) and less code, but the screens feel less instant: tick-boxes for shared items and live totals are harder to make smooth.

# Deep Interview Spec: Bill Splitting Calculator

## Metadata
- Interview ID: b7e2c1a4-5d3f-4e8a-9c21-bill-splitter-01
- Rounds: 10 (plus Round 0 topology check)
- Final Ambiguity Score: 15.1%
- Type: greenfield
- Generated: 2026-10-21
- Threshold: 0.2
- Threshold Source: default
- Initial Context Summarized: no
- Status: PASSED — pending approval

## Clarity Breakdown
| Dimension | Score | Weight | Weighted |
|-----------|-------|--------|----------|
| Goal Clarity | 0.90 | 0.40 | 0.360 |
| Constraint Clarity | 0.87 | 0.30 | 0.261 |
| Success Criteria | 0.76 | 0.30 | 0.228 |
| **Total Clarity** | | | **0.849** |
| **Ambiguity** | | | **0.151** |

## Topology
| Component | Status | Description | Coverage |
|-----------|--------|-------------|----------|
| Solo bill | active | One person totals their own bill (items + tax + tip) and keeps a history | AC-S*, AC-H* |
| Equal group split | active | A bill divided evenly among 2–50 people, cent-exact | AC-E* |
| Itemized group split | active | Each person pays for what they had (items may be shared) plus proportional tax/tip | AC-I* |
| Tech choices and local setup | active | TypeScript, React, Node.js/Express, SQLite; README run with one free install | AC-T* |
| Product docs | active | Roles, jobs to be done, user stories with acceptance criteria and status, kept in line with the app | AC-D* |

## Goal
Build a browser bill-splitting calculator with three separate modes: **Solo**, **Equal split** and **Itemized split**. Every bill can be saved to a history on the user's own computer, and saved bills can be viewed, edited and deleted. All money math is exact to the cent: shares always add up to the bill total. Every invalid input produces a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result. Anyone can run the app from the README with only free, local software.

## Constraints
- Runs in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
- Runs entirely on the reviewer's computer: no paid accounts, API keys, cloud services or internet-only dependencies at runtime.
- One free prerequisite to install: Node.js (current LTS).
- History is stored by a local backend in a SQLite database file inside the project folder (gitignored).
- Three separate modes (user rejected a single unified bill model in Round 4).
- Number limits (all modes):
  - Money: 0.01 to 1,000,000.00, at most 2 decimal places. No negatives, letters, blanks or extra decimals.
  - People in group modes: whole numbers 2–50.
  - Tax % and tip %: 0–100. Amount-mode tax/tip: 0.00–1,000,000.00, 2 decimals.
- Currency: the user picks a display **symbol** per bill from a fixed list (e.g. $, €, £, ¥, ₹, Rs). There is no conversion and one currency per bill. A note next to the picker says it can't be changed once the bill is saved, and it is locked from the first save onward.
- All math uses integer cents internally, never floating-point money.

## Non-Goals
- Currency conversion or multiple currencies on one bill.
- User accounts, login, sharing over the internet, syncing across devices.

## Goal
Build a browser bill-splitting calculator with three separate modes: **Solo**, **Equal split** and **Itemized split**. Every bill can be saved to a history on the user's own computer, and saved bills can be viewed, edited and deleted. All money math is exact to the cent: shares always add up to the bill total. Every invalid input produces a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result. Anyone can run the app from the README with only free, local software.

## Constraints
- Runs in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
- Runs entirely on the reviewer's computer: no paid accounts, API keys, cloud services or internet-only dependencies at runtime.
- One free prerequisite to install: Node.js (current LTS).
- History is stored by a local backend in a SQLite database file inside the project folder (gitignored).

- User accounts, login, sharing over the internet, syncing across devices.
- Payment integration (sending money).
- Receipt scanning / OCR.
- Mobile native apps (responsive web only).

1. **Tax and tip entry:** each has a % / amount switch. Tip may be 0. Percentages are applied to the pre-tax food subtotal, and the resulting cents are rounded half-up.

The leftover cents (total mod N) are given 1 cent each to the first people in list order. The app shows which people pay the extra cent. People default to "Person 1…N" and can be renamed.
3. **Itemized split:**

questions.question:
Round 11 | Part: all three modes | Targeting: Success criteria | Why now: when results appear decides how every acceptance criterion about errors and "carrying on after a result" is written | Ambiguity: 15.1%

When should totals appear?

Cause → effect:
• Calculate button: you fill everything in and press Calculate. Effect: errors only appear when you ask for a result, so you're not shown red messages while still typing. If you change anything afterwards, the old result is hidden until you press Calculate again, so a stale (wrong) number never stays on screen. One extra tap each time.
• Live totals: results update as you type. Effect: feels instant and you can see the effect of changing the tip right away. But half-typed values (like "12." or an empty field) show errors mid-typing, and there are many more moments to test.
• Live totals, quiet errors: results update live, but an error only shows once you leave the field. Effect: smooth and less noisy, but the most work to build and test well.

questions.question:
Round 12 | Part: all modes (tip as %) | Targeting: Goal | Why now: a 15% tip gives a different number depending on what it's 15% of, so the acceptance criteria need one rule | Ambiguity: 13.9%

Example: food $100, tax $10, tip 15%.

Cause → effect:
• Tip on food only (before tax): tip = $15.00, total $125.00. Effect: the most common etiquette (you tip on the service, not the tax). Easy to explain on screen: "15% of food".
• Tip on food + tax: tip = $16.50, total $126.50. Effect: matches some card machines that suggest tips on the full amount. Everyone pays a bit more.
• Let the user choose per bill: a small "tip on: food / food + tax" option. Effect: matches any habit, but it's one more switch and twice the cases to test.

(Tax as a % is always on food only.)

questions.question:
Round 14 | Part: Groups | Targeting: Constraints | Why now: "any member can add a bill" has to work with "no paid accounts, no cloud", and that shapes the whole group feature | Ambiguity: 28.5%

The app and its saved data live on one computer. How do group members add bills?

Cause → effect:
• Shared device, no logins: whoever has the app open adds the bill and picks from the member list who paid and who was there. Members are just names, and a member "not on the app" is simply a name in the group. Effect: works fully offline, needs no accounts, and is exactly what a reviewer can test on one computer. Downside: friends can't add bills from their own phones unless they use that same computer.
• Same Wi-Fi access: the same as above, plus friends on the same Wi-Fi can open the app from their phones using the host computer's address. Still no cloud and no accounts. Effect: closer to "everyone can add", but it only works while the host computer is on and everyone is on the same network. Extra README steps, a bit more to test, and anyone on that Wi-Fi can see and edit the data.
• Real accounts for each member: each person logs in on their own device. Effect: true multi-user, but it needs an internet server, which breaks your "no cloud services" rule.

questions.question:
Round 15 | Part: Groups | Targeting: Goal | Why now: with lasting groups, the app is either a per-bill calculator or a running record of who owes whom, and that decides most screens and stories | Ambiguity: 35%

When a group bill is added, what should the app track?

Cause → effect:
• Who paid + running balances: each bill records who paid it (e.g. Ali paid $65). The app keeps a running balance per member across all the group's bills ("Sara owes Ali $13", "Omar is owed $20"), and a "settle up" records a repayment. Effect: answers "who owes whom" after many outings, like Splitwise. Much more value, but more to build: payers, balances, settle-ups and simplified debts. Every balance must still add up to zero exactly.
• Shares only, per bill: each bill shows what each person owes for that bill, and that's it. No payer and no running totals. Effect: simpler, and every bill stands alone. But after five dinners the group has to add things up themselves.
• Shares + payer, no settle-up: records who paid and shows per-bill "X owes Y", but no running total across bills. Effect: a middle ground, but it doesn't answer the overall question either.

Who can pay a group bill, and how are balances shown?

Cause → effect:
• One payer per bill + simplified "who pays whom": each bill has exactly one payer, chosen from the members who took part (or any group member). The balance screen shows each member's net amount (+ is owed, − owes), plus the fewest payments needed to settle everyone (e.g. "Sara pays Ali 13.00"). Effect: covers most real outings, the totals always net to exactly zero, and the payment list is short.
• Several payers per bill: e.g. Ali paid $40 and Sara paid $25 of one bill. Effect: handles split card payments at the till, but it's another set of numbers that must add up to the bill, with more errors to check and more to test.
• One payer, no simplification: shows every pairwise debt from every bill ("Sara owes Ali 13", "Ali owes Sara 5"). Effect: easier to trace back to each bill, but the list gets long and people pay each other back and forth.

# Deep Interview Spec: Bill Splitting Calculator (v2)

## Metadata
- Interview ID: b7e2c1a4-5d3f-4e8a-9c21-bill-splitter-01
- Rounds: 19 (plus Round 0 topology check)
- Final Ambiguity Score: 17.6%
- Type: greenfield
- Generated: 2026-10-21 (v2 replaces the v1 spec written after Round 10)
- Threshold: 0.2
- Threshold Source: default
- Initial Context Summarized: no
- Status: PASSED — pending approval

## Clarity Breakdown
| Dimension | Score | Weight | Weighted |
|-----------|-------|--------|----------|
| Goal Clarity | 0.86 | 0.40 | 0.344 |
| Constraint Clarity | 0.84 | 0.30 | 0.252 |
| Success Criteria | 0.76 | 0.30 | 0.228 |
| **Total Clarity** | | | **0.824** |
| **Ambiguity** | | | **0.176** |

## Topology
| Component | Status | Description | Coverage |
|-----------|--------|-------------|----------|
| Solo bill | active | A logged-in person totals their own bill and keeps a private history | AC-S, AC-H |
| Equal group split | active | A group bill split evenly between the members who took part, cent-exact | AC-E |
| Itemized group split | active | Each participant pays for what they had (items can be shared) plus proportional tax and tip | AC-I |
| Groups (added R13) | active | Lasting friend groups: name-only or claimed members, payer, running balances, settle-ups, activity log | AC-G |
| Accounts (added R14) | active | In-app username/password accounts with a recovery code; no outside services | AC-A |
| Tech choices and setup | active | TypeScript, React, Node.js/Express, SQLite; runs locally from the README and deploys to any server | AC-T |
| Product docs | active | Roles, jobs and stories in the saved format, kept in line with the app | AC-D |

## Goal
A self-contained web app for splitting and tracking bills:
- **Solo diners** total their own bills (items, tax and tip) and keep a private history.
- **Friends** form lasting groups. Any member can record a group bill: who paid, who took part, and whether it's split equally or by items. The app keeps exact running balances, shows the fewest payments needed to settle up, and records settle-ups.

All money math is exact to the cent, and every invalid input gives a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result.

## Constraints
- **Browsers:** current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
- **No third-party services:** the app must not depend on any external cloud or paid service (no hosted auth, hosted database, email/SMS or payment APIs). It **can** be deployed to a server. Reviewers must be able to run it locally from the README with only free software (Node.js LTS).
- **Accounts:** built into the app. Username + password, with passwords hashed. Sessions use secure cookies. No email anywhere.
- **Storage:** SQLite database file managed by the app's own server.
- **Modes:** Solo (personal), Group bill with Equal split, and Group bill with Itemized split. These are separate screens and rules (Round 4).
- **Number limits:**
  - Money: 0.01–1,000,000.00, at most 2 decimal places. No negatives, letters, blanks or extra decimals.
  - Group size: 2–50 members.
  - Tax and tip %: 0–100. Tax and tip amounts: 0.00–1,000,000.00.
- **Currency:** a display symbol only, picked from a fixed list (e.g. $, €, £, ¥, ₹, Rs), with no conversion.
  - Each **group** has one currency, chosen at creation and never changeable. A note says so when you choose it.
  - Each **solo bill** has its own currency, locked when the bill is first saved.
- **Math:** integer cents only, never floating-point money.
- **Results:** totals appear when the user presses **Calculate**. Changing any input hides the old result until Calculate is pressed again.

## Non-Goals
- Currency conversion; multiple currencies in one group.
- Email or SMS (invites, password resets, notifications).
- Real payment processing (settle-ups are records only).
- Receipt scanning, native mobile apps, real-time push updates.
- Multiple payers on one bill (Round 19).

## Calculation Rules
1. **Tax:** a % (of the food subtotal) or an amount.
2. **Tip:** a % or an amount. Tip may be 0. For a % tip, each bill has a "tip on" option: **food only (default)** or **food + tax**. Percent results are rounded half-up to the cent.
3. **Equal split:** grand total ÷ number of participants. Leftover cents go 1 each to the first participants in list order, and the app shows who pays the extra cent.
4. **Itemized split:**
   - Each item has a price and 1+ ticked participants. Its cost is split evenly between them, with leftover cents going to the first ticked people.
   - Tax and tip are split in proportion to each participant's food subtotal, with leftover cents assigned by largest remainder.
   - A participant with no items owes 0.00.
5. **Group balances:**
   - Each group bill has one payer, who can be any current group member.
   - The payer is credited with the full grand total, and each participant is debited their share.
   - A settle-up from A to B credits A and debits B.
   - Net balances across the group always sum to exactly 0.00.
6. **Settle-up suggestions:** the fewest payments that bring every net balance to zero (greedy match of largest debtor to largest creditor), shown as "X pays Y amount".
7. **Invariant:** for every bill, the shares sum exactly to the grand total.

## Acceptance Criteria
### Accounts (AC-A)
- [ ] Given a new username and a valid password, when I sign up, then my account is created, a one-time recovery code is shown with a "save this now" warning, and I'm logged in.
- [ ] Given a username that is already taken, when I sign up, then I see "That username is taken" and no account is created.
- [ ] Given a wrong password, when I log in, then I see "Username or password is incorrect" (without saying which one) and I stay logged out.
- [ ] Given my username + recovery code + a new password, when I reset, then I can log in with the new password, the old code stops working, and a new code is shown.
- [ ] Given I'm logged out, when I open any bill or group page, then I'm sent to login and no data is shown.
- [ ] Given I'm logged in, I can never see or change another account's solo bills, or groups I'm not a member of, even by typing the address directly.

### Solo (AC-S)
- [ ] Given items 12.50 and 7.50, tax 10%, tip 15% on food, when I press Calculate, then subtotal 20.00, tax 2.00, tip 3.00 and total 25.00 are shown.
- [ ] Given food 100.00, tax 10.00 (amount) and tip 15% on food + tax, then the tip is 16.50 and the total is 126.50.
- [ ] Given tip 0, then the tip shows 0.00 with no error.
- [ ] Given no items, when I press Calculate, then I see "Add at least one item" and no result.

### Equal group split (AC-E)
- [ ] Given total 100.00 with 3 participants, then the shares are 33.34 / 33.33 / 33.33, the first participant is marked as paying the extra cent, and the shares sum to 100.00.
- [ ] Given 0 participants selected, when I press Calculate, then I see "Choose who took part" and no result (no division by zero).
- [ ] Given 0.01 split between 2 participants, then the shares are 0.01 and 0.00.
- [ ] Given 1,000,000.00 with a 100% tip split between 50 participants, then the shares are exact and sum to the total.

### Itemized group split (AC-I)
- [ ] Given Ali steak 40.00, Sara salad 10.00, tax 5.00 and tip 10.00, then Ali's share is 52.00 and Sara's is 13.00.
- [ ] Given nachos 12.00 ticked for Ali, Sara and Omar, then each is charged 4.00 for it, and 10.00 shared by 3 gives 3.34 / 3.33 / 3.33.
- [ ] Given an item with nobody ticked, when I press Calculate, then I see "Choose who shared this item" and no result.
- [ ] For any valid bill, the per-person totals sum exactly to the grand total.

### Groups (AC-G)
- [ ] Given I create a group with a name and a currency, then I'm its first member, I see a note that the currency can't be changed, and the group has an invite code.
- [ ] Given a group of 10 members, when I add a bill with 5 participants, then only those 5 are charged and the other 5 balances don't change.
- [ ] Given Ali paid 65.00 and Ali 52.00 / Sara 13.00 are the shares, then Ali's net balance is +13.00, Sara's is −13.00, and the suggestion reads "Sara pays Ali 13.00".

## Goal
A self-contained web app for splitting and tracking bills:
- **Solo diners** total their own bills (items, tax and tip) and keep a private history.
- **Friends** form lasting groups. Any member can record a group bill: who paid, who took part, and whether it's split equally or by items. The app keeps exact running balances, shows the fewest payments needed to settle up, and records settle-ups.

All money math is exact to the cent, and every invalid input gives a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result.

## Constraints
- **Browsers:** current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.

- **Accounts:** built into the app. Username + password, with passwords hashed. Sessions use secure cookies. No email anywhere.
- **Storage:** SQLite database file managed by the app's own server.
- **Modes:** Solo (personal), Group bill with Equal split, and Group bill with Itemized split. These are separate screens and rules (Round 4).
- **Number limits:**

  - Group size: 2–50 members.

- **Currency:** a display symbol only, picked from a fixed list (e.g. $, €, £, ¥, ₹, Rs), with no conversion.

  - Each **solo bill** has its own currency, locked when the bill is first saved.
- **Math:** integer cents only, never floating-point money.
- **Results:** totals appear when the user presses **Calculate**. Changing any input hides the old result until Calculate is pressed again.

- Currency conversion; multiple currencies in one group.
- Email or SMS (invites, password resets, notifications).
- Real payment processing (settle-ups are records only).

## Goal
A self-contained web app for splitting and tracking bills:
- **Solo diners** total their own bills (items, tax and tip) and keep a private history.
- **Friends** form lasting groups. Any member can record a group bill: who paid, who took part, and whether it's split equally or by items. The app keeps exact running balances, shows the fewest payments needed to settle up, and records settle-ups.

All money math is exact to the cent, and every invalid input gives a clear message, never a crash or a wrong result.

## Constraints
- **Browsers:** current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari.
- **No third-party services:** the app must not depend on any external cloud or paid service (no hosted auth, hosted database, email/SMS or payment APIs). It **can** be deployed to a server. Reviewers must be able to run it locally from the README with only free software (Node.js LTS).
- **Accounts:** built into the app. Username + password, with passwords hashed. Sessions use secure cookies. No email anywhere.
- **Storage:** SQLite database file managed by the app's own server.
- **Modes:** Solo (personal), Group bill with Equal split, and Group bill with Itemized split. These are separate screens and rules (Round 4).
- **Number limits:**
  - Money: 0.01–1,000,000.00, at most 2 decimal places. No negatives, letters, blanks or extra decimals.
  - Group size: 2–50 members.
  - Tax and tip %: 0–100. Tax and tip amounts: 0.00–1,000,000.00.
- **Currency:** a display symbol only, picked from a fixed list (e.g. $, €, £, ¥, ₹, Rs), with no conversion.
  - Each **group** has one currency, chosen at creation and never changeable. A note says so when you choose it.
  - Each **solo bill** has its own currency, locked when the bill is first saved.
- **Math:** integer cents only, never floating-point money.
- **Results:** totals appear when the user presses **Calculate**. Changing any input hides the old result until Calculate is pressed again.

## Non-Goals
- Currency conversion; multiple currencies in one group.
- Email or SMS (invites, password resets, notifications).
- Real payment processing (settle-ups are records only).
- Receipt scanning, native mobile apps, real-time push updates.
- Multiple payers on one bill (Round 19).

## Calculation Rules
1. **Tax:** a % (of the food subtotal) or an amount.
2. **Tip:** a % or an amount. Tip may be 0. For a % tip, each bill has a "tip on" option: **food only (default)** or **food + tax**. Percent results are rounded half-up to the cent.
3. **Equal split:** grand total ÷ number of participants. Leftover cents go 1 each to the first participants in list order, and the app shows who pays the extra cent.
4. **Itemized split:**
   - Each item has a price and 1+ ticked participants. Its cost is split evenly between them, with leftover cents going to the first ticked people.
   - Tax and tip are split in proportion to each participant's food subtotal, with leftover cents assigned by largest remainder.
   - A participant with no items owes 0.00.
5. **Group balances:**
   - Each group bill has one payer, who can be any current group member.
   - The payer is credited with the full grand total, and each participant is debited their share.
   - A settle-up from A to B credits A and debits B.
   - Net balances across the group always sum to exactly 0.00.
6. **Settle-up suggestions:** the fewest payments that bring every net balance to zero (greedy match of largest debtor to largest creditor), shown as "X pays Y amount".
7. **Invariant:** for every bill, the shares sum exactly to the grand total.

## Acceptance Criteria
### Accounts (AC-A)
- [ ] Given a new username and a valid password, when I sign up, then my account is created, a one-time recovery code is shown with a "save this now" warning, and I'm logged in.
- [ ] Given a username that is already taken, when I sign up, then I see "That username is taken" and no account is created.
- [ ] Given a wrong password, when I log in, then I see "Username or password is incorrect" (without saying which one) and I stay logged out.
- [ ] Given my username + recovery code + a new password, when I reset, then I can log in with the new password, the old code stops working, and a new code is shown.
- [ ] Given I'm logged out, when I open any bill or group page, then I'm sent to login and no data is shown.
- [ ] Given I'm logged in, I can never see or change another account's solo bills, or groups I'm not a member of, even by typing the address directly.

### Solo (AC-S)
- [ ] Given items 12.50 and 7.50, tax 10%, tip 15% on food, when I press Calculate, then subtotal 20.00, tax 2.00, tip 3.00 and total 25.00 are shown.
- [ ] Given food 100.00, tax 10.00 (amount) and tip 15% on food + tax, then the tip is 16.50 and the total is 126.50.
- [ ] Given tip 0, then the tip shows 0.00 with no error.
- [ ] Given no items, when I press Calculate, then I see "Add at least one item" and no result.

### Equal group split (AC-E)
- [ ] Given total 100.00 with 3 participants, then the shares are 33.34 / 33.33 / 33.33, the first participant is marked as paying the extra cent, and the shares sum to 100.00.
- [ ] Given 0 participants selected, when I press Calculate, then I see "Choose who took part" and no result (no division by zero).
- [ ] Given 0.01 split between 2 participants, then the shares are 0.01 and 0.00.
- [ ] Given 1,000,000.00 with a 100% tip split between 50 participants, then the shares are exact and sum to the total.

### Itemized group split (AC-I)
- [ ] Given Ali steak 40.00, Sara salad 10.00, tax 5.00 and tip 10.00, then Ali's share is 52.00 and Sara's is 13.00.
- [ ] Given nachos 12.00 ticked for Ali, Sara and Omar, then each is charged 4.00 for it, and 10.00 shared by 3 gives 3.34 / 3.33 / 3.33.
- [ ] Given an item with nobody ticked, when I press Calculate, then I see "Choose who shared this item" and no result.
- [ ] For any valid bill, the per-person totals sum exactly to the grand total.

### Groups (AC-G)
- [ ] Given I create a group with a name and a currency, then I'm its first member, I see a note that the currency can't be changed, and the group has an invite code.
- [ ] Given a group of 10 members, when I add a bill with 5 participants, then only those 5 are charged and the other 5 balances don't change.
- [ ] Given Ali paid 65.00 and Ali 52.00 / Sara 13.00 are the shares, then Ali's net balance is +13.00, Sara's is −13.00, and the suggestion reads "Sara pays Ali 13.00".
- [ ] Given net balances across the group, they always sum to exactly 0.00.
- [ ] Given I record "Sara paid Ali 13.00", then both balances become 0.00 and the suggestion disappears.
- [ ] Given I add a name-only member "Omar", then Omar can be a participant or payer right away.
- [ ] Given Omar signs up and enters the group's invite code, when he chooses "I'm Omar", then his account is linked to that member and he sees the full group history.
- [ ] Given a member already claimed by an account, another account can't claim it, and the same account can't claim two members in one group.
- [ ] Given a wrong invite code, then I see "That invite code isn't valid" and join nothing.
- [ ] Given any member edits or deletes a bill or settle-up, then the balances update, and the activity log shows who did it, when, and what changed.
- [ ] Given deleting a bill, then a confirmation is asked first. Cancel keeps the bill.
- [ ] Given a member whose balance isn't 0.00, when anyone tries to remove them, then I see "Settle this member's balance before removing them" and nothing changes.
- [ ] Given a group with 50 members, when I add another, then I see "A group can have at most 50 members".

### Input validation & recovery (all modes)
- [ ] Given a money field containing "abc", "-5", "1.234", "1000000.01" or a blank, then a message next to the field explains the rule and no result is shown.
- [ ] Given tax or tip % outside 0–100, then a clear message is shown and no result.
- [ ] Given an error is showing, when I fix the field and press Calculate, then the error clears and the correct result appears, with no reload needed.
- [ ] Given a result is showing, when I change any input, then the old result is hidden until I press Calculate again.
- [ ] The app never shows NaN, Infinity, "undefined" or a blank/crashed screen, and the server rejects invalid data even when it's sent directly, bypassing the page.
- [ ] Given the server can't be reached, when I save, then I see "Couldn't save — check your connection" and my inputs are kept.

### History (AC-H)
- [ ] Given I save a solo bill, then it appears at the top of my history with name, date, currency and total. The name is optional and defaults to "Bill – date".
- [ ] Given a saved solo bill, I can open it, edit it (with the same validation and recalculation as a new bill, and the currency locked) and delete it after a confirmation.
- [ ] Given the server restarts, then all bills, groups and balances are still there.

### Tech & setup (AC-T)
- [ ] With Node.js LTS installed, a fresh clone plus the README steps (install, start, open URL) gives a working app, and I can sign up locally. No outside service, key or account is needed.
- [ ] The same build runs on a server, configured only through settings the app owns (port, database file location, session secret).
- [ ] Calculation and validation tests plus browser tests (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) pass with one command.

### Product docs (AC-D)
- [ ] docs/ follows the saved format rules: role/job/story templates, story → job → role links, Given/When/Then acceptance criteria, and Implemented / Not implemented status.
- [ ] Every story marked Implemented passes its acceptance criteria in the running app.

## Roles (for docs)
- **Solo diner:** eats or shops alone and wants an accurate personal total and a private record of spending. Must never see other people's bills, or have their solo bills seen by anyone else.
- **Group member:** belongs to one or more friend groups, all with equal rights. Can add, edit or delete group bills and settle-ups, add name-only friends, and see balances. Must never see groups they aren't in, remove a member who still owes or is owed, or change a group's currency.
- Friends who never sign up exist only as **name-only members**. They are data, not a role.

## Technical Context
- **Language:** TypeScript (frontend and backend), with a shared pure calculation module that works in integer cents and is used by both the page and the server.
- **Frontend:** React built with Vite. **Backend:** Node.js LTS + Express, serving the API and the built frontend from one process (easy to deploy).
- **Database:** SQLite file; prefer Node's built-in `node:sqlite` so no native build step is needed.
- **Auth:** password hashing with Node's built-in `crypto.scrypt`, server-side sessions in an httpOnly, SameSite cookie, and login rate limiting done in-app.
- **Tests:** Vitest (calculation, validation and API) and Playwright (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit).
- **Layout:** `src/` (client, server, shared), `tests/`, `docs/`, `transcripts/`, README.

## Ontology (Key Entities)
| Entity | Type | Fields | Relationships |
|--------|------|--------|---------------|
| Account | core | username, passwordHash, recoveryCodeHash | owns SoloBills; claims Members |
| Group | core | name, currency, inviteCode | has Members, GroupBills, SettleUps, ActivityEntries |
| Member | core | displayName, accountId? (null = name-only) | belongs to Group; participant/payer in GroupBills |
| SoloBill | core | name, currency, items, tax, tip, tipBase | belongs to Account |
| GroupBill | core | name, splitMode (equal/itemized), payer, participants, items, tax, tip, tipBase | belongs to Group |
| Item | core | name, priceCents, sharers | belongs to a bill |
| Share | derived | memberId, food/tax/tip/total cents, extraCent | computed per participant |
| SettleUp | core | from, to, amountCents, date | belongs to Group |
| Balance | derived | memberId, netCents | computed from GroupBills + SettleUps |
| SuggestedPayment | derived | from, to, amountCents | computed from Balances |
| ActivityEntry | supporting | who, when, action, before/after | belongs to Group |
| Currency, Tax, Tip | supporting | symbol; mode + value | on Group/bills |

## Open Assumptions (confirm while planning, low risk)
- The payer can be any current group member, even one who didn't take part in the bill.
- A settle-up can be any valid amount, even more than is owed, and the balances simply update.
- Removed members (balance 0) stay visible on their old bills, marked "(removed)".
- Any member can view and regenerate the group's invite code.
- There's no group-less quick split: a one-off group outing means creating a group.

content.text:
I've sent you the spec file above. It's saved at [.omc/specs/deep-interview-bill-splitter.md](.omc/specs/deep-interview-bill-splitter.md). Nothing has been built yet.

**What's in it:**
- **The app:** solo diners track their own bills privately. Friends form lasting groups where any member can add a bill, choose who paid and who took part, and split it equally or by items. Shared dishes are allowed.
- **Money rules:** all math is exact to the cent, and shares always add up to the bill. Tax and tip can each be a % or an amount, and the tip base is chosen per bill. Each group has one currency symbol that can't be changed.
- **Groups:** running balances, the fewest payments needed to settle up, and recorded settle-ups. All members are equal and every change is logged. Friends can be added by name and claim their spot later with an invite code.
- **Accounts:** username and password, with a one-time recovery code instead of email.
- **Limits and errors:** amounts from 0.01 to 1,000,000, groups of 2–50 people, and tax/tip from 0–100%. Every bad input gets a clear message, and results only appear when you press Calculate.
- **Tech:** TypeScript, React, Node.js/Express and SQLite. It runs locally from the README with only Node.js installed, and can be deployed to any server.
- **Acceptance criteria:** Given/When/Then checks for each part, ready to become your user stories.

**Saved to memory:** what "no cloud services" means here. The app can't depend on outside or paid services, but it can be deployed to a server.

**Still open:** five small assumptions, listed near the end of the spec, such as whether someone who didn't eat can be the payer. They're easy to confirm before building.

The `.omc` folder is gitignored, so the spec is on your computer but not in your repo.

questions.question:
When other charges are a %, what is it a percentage OF? Example: food 100.00, tax 10.00, other charges 5%.
• Food subtotal: 5.00. Same base as tax, so the simplest and most predictable.
• Food + tax: 5.50.
• Food + tax + tip: depends on the tip, which can go in circles if the tip is also based on other charges.

options.label: Food subtotal (Recommended)
options.description: Same base as tax %. 5% of 100.00 food = 5.00.

options.label: Food + tax + tip
options.description: Percentage of everything else. Tip must then never be based on other charges.

questions.question:
Is the other charges field optional, and what values are allowed?
• Optional (recommended): the field can be left empty or set to 0, meaning no other charges. If entered as an amount it must be 0.01–1,000,000.00 (2 decimals). As a %, 0.01–100.
• Required: every bill must have other charges of at least 0.01. Most restaurant bills have none, so this would force people to invent a value.

options.label: Optional, 0 = none (Recommended)
options.description: Blank or 0 means no other charges. Otherwise amount 0.01–1,000,000.00 or % 0.01–100.

options.label: Optional, % allows 0–100
options.description: Same as above, but treat 0% exactly like tax and tip (0–100 allowed).

options.label: Required, min 0.01
options.description: Every bill must include other charges.

questions.question:
Each bill has a 'tip on' option (food only / food + tax). Should the tip ever be calculated on other charges too?
• Never: the tip options stay 'food only' and 'food + tax'. Other charges (e.g. service or delivery fees) are not tipped on.
• Add a third option: 'food + tax + other charges'. More flexible, but one more case to test.

options.label: Never tip on other charges (Recommended)
options.description: Tip options stay food only (default) or food + tax.

options.label: Add third tip option
options.description: Tip on: food only / food + tax / food + tax + other charges.

questions.question:
In an itemized group split, how are other charges shared between participants?
• Proportional to food, like tax and tip: someone who ordered 80% of the food pays 80% of other charges.
• Split equally between all participants: suits fixed fees such as a table or delivery fee, but the person who ate less pays relatively more.

options.label: Proportional to food (Recommended)
options.description: Same rule as tax and tip. Leftover cents by largest remainder.

options.label: Split equally
options.description: Each participant pays the same share of other charges. Leftover cents go to the first participants.
